title: Λουτρὸν καὶ λέχος
titleEn: The Bath and the Bed — Odyssey 23.97–182
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Telemachus scolds his mother for sitting apart from the stranger who is her husband, and Penelope answers that her heart is stunned and she cannot speak to him or look him in the face; if it is truly Odysseus, she says, the two of them have private signs by which they will know each other. Odysseus smiles, tells his son to let her test him, and turns to the matter of the dead suitors: a man who kills even one fellow citizen goes into exile, and they have killed the best young men of Ithaca. Telemachus leaves the plan to his father's cunning, and Odysseus lays it out. They are to bathe and dress, and the minstrel is to lead a dance so that anyone passing will take it for a wedding, so that no report of the killing spreads before they can leave for the farm. The household does as he says, and a passer-by is deceived. Eurynome bathes Odysseus, and Athena makes him taller and sturdier and pours grace over him, so that he steps out of the bath like an immortal. He sits down opposite Penelope and reproaches her for her iron heart, and asks for a bed to be made up for him. Penelope, testing him, tells Eurycleia to carry his bed out of the chamber he built himself and to make it up there. Odysseus, vexed, begins to answer her as the part ends.

sentences.l:
“Mother mine, ill-mother, an unkind heart having,
why thus from your father do you hold aloof, nor beside him
sitting with words do you question him, nor inquire?
sentences.i: “Mother, my unnatural mother, with a heart so unkind, why do you keep yourself aloof from your father like this, and do not sit beside him to question him and inquire?
sentences.n: Telemachus is speaking; the narrator introduced the speech in the last line of the previous part, so the opening quotation mark falls here. μῆτερ ἐμή is 'my mother'. δύσμητερ is built from δυσ- 'ill, bad' and μήτηρ: 'bad mother', that is, a mother who does not act as one. ἀπηνέα θυμὸν ἔχουσα is 'having an unkind heart': ἀπηνής 'unkind, harsh', and θυμόν is the object of the participle ἔχουσα. τίφθ’ is τίπτε 'why' before the rough breathing of οὕτω: elision turns π and τ into φ and θ. νοσφίζεαι is the middle of νοσφίζω 'turn away from, keep apart from', with the genitive πατρός; its ending -εαι is uncontracted (Attic -ῃ). ἑζομένη is the participle of ἕζομαι 'sit', and παρ’ αὐτὸν is 'beside him'. ἀνείρεαι and μεταλλᾷς are the two verbs 'question' and 'inquire after', both second person singular, the second contracted.

sentences.t:
οὐ μέν κ’ ἄλλη γ’ ὧδε γυνὴ τετληότι θυμῷ
ἀνδρὸς ἀφεσταίη, ὅς οἱ κακὰ πολλὰ μογήσας
ἔλθοι ἐεικοστῷ ἔτεϊ ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν·
sentences.tr:
ou men k’ allē g’ hōde gynē tetlēoti thymōi
andros aphestaiē, hos hoi kaka polla mogēsas
elthoi eeikostōi eteï es patrida gaian·
sentences.i: No other woman would hold aloof from her husband like this, with an enduring heart, when he had come to his fatherland in the twentieth year after toiling through many evils;
sentences.n: These three lines come back word for word at lines 168 to 170, where Odysseus says them to Penelope, and the English is kept the same so that the repetition is heard. οὐ μέν κε … ἀφεσταίη is a potential optative, 'would not … stand aloof' (κε = ἄν); ἀφεσταίη is the aorist optative of ἀφίστημι in its intransitive sense and takes the genitive ἀνδρός, 'from her husband'. ὧδε is 'thus, so'. τετληότι θυμῷ is 'with enduring heart': τετληότι is the perfect participle of τλῆναι 'endure', in the dative with θυμῷ. ὅς … ἔλθοι is a relative clause with the optative (it follows the potential optative of the main clause); the dative οἱ is a dative of interest, which English drops; whom it points to (the husband himself, or the wife) the Greek leaves open. μογήσας is the aorist participle of μογέω 'toil, suffer'. ἐεικοστῷ ἔτεϊ is 'in the twentieth year': ἐεικοστῷ is the epic form of εἰκοστῷ, and ἔτεϊ the dative of ἔτος. πατρίδα γαῖαν is 'fatherland'.

sentences.t: σοὶ δ’ αἰεὶ κραδίη στερεωτέρη ἐστὶ λίθοιο.
sentences.tr: soi d’ aiei kradiē stereōterē esti lithoio.
sentences.l: but to you always a heart is harder than stone.”
sentences.i: but your heart is always harder than stone.”
sentences.n: The last line of Telemachus's speech; the closing quotation mark falls here. σοί is a dative of possession, 'you have'. αἰεί is the epic form of ἀεί. κραδίη is the epic form of καρδία 'heart'. στερεωτέρη is the comparative of στερεός 'hard, firm', and λίθοιο, a genitive in -οιο (Attic λίθου), is the genitive of comparison: 'harder than stone'. The image of a hard heart is taken up in Odysseus's words at 172, where her heart is iron.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe periphrōn Pēnelopeia·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The formula that brings Penelope in to answer her son. τὸν is the pronoun 'him' (in Homer the article is a pronoun), αὖτε is 'in turn, again', and προσέειπε is the aorist of προσεῖπον 'speak to, address', a reply verb distinct from ἠμείβετο 'answered'. περίφρων 'circumspect' is her stock epithet, from περί (here 'exceedingly, all round') and φρήν 'mind'; it is translated the same way every time, wherever the context.

sentences.t:
τέκνον ἐμόν, θυμός μοι ἐνὶ στήθεσσι τέθηπεν,
οὐδέ τι προσφάσθαι δύναμαι ἔπος οὐδ’ ἐρέεσθαι
οὐδ’ εἰς ὦπα ἰδέσθαι ἐναντίον.
sentences.tr:
teknon emon, thymos moi eni stēthessi tethēpen,
oude ti prosphasthai dynamai epos oud’ ereesthai
oud’ eis ōpa idesthai enantion.
sentences.l:
“My child, my heart in my breast is stunned,
and not at all am I able to speak a word, nor to ask a question,
nor to look into his face, opposite him.
sentences.i: “My child, the heart in my breast is stunned; I cannot say a word to him, nor question him, nor look him straight in the face.
sentences.n: Penelope answers her son. τέκνον ἐμόν is 'my child'. θυμός is 'heart'; μοι is the dative 'my' (a dative of interest), and ἐνὶ στήθεσσι is 'in the breast', στήθεσσι being the dative plural of στῆθος in -εσσι. τέθηπεν is the perfect, with present sense, of an old verb related to the noun τάφος 'amazement': 'is struck dumb, is stunned'. δύναμαι takes three infinitives: προσφάσθαι 'to speak to' (with the object ἔπος 'a word'), ἐρέεσθαι 'to ask' (uncontracted; Attic ἐρέσθαι), and ἰδέσθαι 'to look'. εἰς ὦπα ἰδέσθαι is 'to look into the face': ὦπα is the accusative of ὤψ 'face, eye'. ἐναντίον is 'opposite, face to face'. The full stop falls in the middle of line 107.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἐτεὸν δὴ
ἔστ’ Ὀδυσεὺς καὶ οἶκον ἱκάνεται, ἦ μάλα νῶϊ
γνωσόμεθ’ ἀλλήλων καὶ λώϊον·
sentences.tr:
ei d’ eteon dē
est’ Odyseus kai oikon hikanetai, ē mala nōï
gnōsometh’ allēlōn kai lōïon·
sentences.i: But if it truly is Odysseus, and he has come home, then we two shall surely know each other, and in a better way;
sentences.n: εἰ δ’ ἐτεὸν δή is 'but if it is indeed true': ἐτεόν is the neuter of ἐτεός 'true' used as an adverb. ἔστ’ is ἔστι, 'it is', so 'if it really is Odysseus'. ἱκάνεται is the present middle of ἱκάνω 'come to, arrive at', with οἶκον as its goal; the present describes the arrival as a state. ἦ μάλα is 'truly, very surely'. νῶϊ is the dual 'we two', the subject of the plural verb γνωσόμεθα (future of γιγνώσκω); ἀλλήλων 'each other' is a genitive plural. λώϊον is the comparative of ἀγαθός, 'better': the recognition she has in mind is one that does not depend on looks, and the reason follows in the next unit. The stop in the middle of line 109 ends this unit.

sentences.t:
ἔστι γὰρ ἡμῖν
σήμαθ’, ἃ δὴ καὶ νῶϊ κεκρυμμένα ἴδμεν ἀπ’ ἄλλων.
sentences.tr:
esti gar hēmin
sēmath’, ha dē kai nōï kekrymmena idmen ap’ allōn.
sentences.l:
for there are for us
signs, which indeed we two also know, hidden from others.”
sentences.i: for we have signs, which we two also know, hidden from everyone else.”
sentences.n: ἔστι γάρ gives the reason: the signs are what will let them know each other. ἡμῖν is a dative of possession, 'we have', and σήματα are 'signs, tokens' by which a person can be recognised. ἃ δὴ καὶ νῶϊ … ἴδμεν: the relative ἅ has σήματα as its antecedent; νῶϊ is the dual 'we two', and ἴδμεν is the epic first person plural of οἶδα (Attic ἴσμεν). κεκρυμμένα is the perfect passive participle of κρύπτω 'hide', agreeing with σήματα. ἀπ’ ἄλλων is 'from others'. The closing quotation mark falls here, at the end of Penelope's speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, μείδησεν δὲ πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
αἶψα δὲ Τηλέμαχον ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, meidēsen de polytlas dios Odysseus,
aipsa de Tēlemachon epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and smiled, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus,
and at once, to Telemachus, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus smiled, and at once spoke winged words to Telemachus:
sentences.n: The narrator turns from Penelope's speech to Odysseus: he smiles, and it is Telemachus, not his wife, whom he addresses. ὣς φάτο is 'so she spoke', the third person singular of φημί without augment; 'she' because Penelope is the speaker. μείδησεν is the aorist of μειδάω 'smile'. πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is a stock phrase, translated every time: πολύτλας is πολυ- 'much' with τλῆναι 'endure', 'much-enduring', and δῖος is 'heavenly'. αἶψα is 'at once'. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the formula 'spoke winged words': προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω 'speak to', and the words are 'winged' because they fly from speaker to hearer. The line ends in ·, introducing the speech that follows.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, ἦ τοι μητέρ’ ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἔασον
πειράζειν ἐμέθεν·
sentences.tr:
Tēlemach’, ē toi mēter’ eni megaroisin eason
peirazein emethen·
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, truly, your mother in the halls allow
to make trial of me;
sentences.i: “Telemachus, let your mother test me in the halls;
sentences.n: Odysseus's speech to Telemachus begins. Τηλέμαχ’ is the vocative with its final vowel elided; ἦ τοι is 'truly, indeed'. ἔασον is the aorist imperative of ἐάω 'allow'. πειράζειν is the infinitive of πειράζω (Attic πειρᾶν), 'make trial of, test', and the verb takes the genitive: ἐμέθεν is the epic genitive of ἐγώ (= ἐμοῦ), 'of me'. ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν is 'in the halls': ἐνί is ἐν, the dative plural ends in -οισιν, and the plural stands for one house. Odysseus is telling his son to let Penelope go on testing him in her own way. The · after ἐμέθεν ends the unit in the middle of line 114.

sentences.t: τάχα δὲ φράσεται καὶ ἄρειον.
sentences.tr: tacha de phrasetai kai areion.
sentences.l: and soon she will observe, and better.
sentences.i: and soon she will observe better.
sentences.n: τάχα is 'soon' (an adverb of ταχύς). φράσεται is the future middle of φράζω; the middle means 'observe, take note, consider'. ἄρειον is the neuter of the comparative ἀρείων 'better'. The Greek leaves the object and the exact sense open, so that the words can be read as 'she will observe better' or 'she will think of something better'; the English keeps the first reading, the one nearer the literal line. Odysseus is asking for patience.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ὅττι ῥυπόω, κακὰ δὲ χροῒ εἵματα εἷμαι,
τοὔνεκ’ ἀτιμάζει με καὶ οὔ πω φησὶ τὸν εἶναι.
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ hotti rhypoō, kaka de chroï heimata heimai,
tounek’ atimazei me kai ou pō phēsi ton einai.
sentences.l:
But now because I am filthy, and bad clothes upon my skin I wear,
for that reason she dishonours me, and not yet does she say that I am he.
sentences.i: Now because I am filthy and wear shabby clothes on my body, she dishonours me for that, and does not yet say that I am he.
sentences.n: Odysseus explains why Penelope does not yet accept him. ὅττι is the epic ὅτι 'because', with doubled τ. ῥυπόω is the epic -όω form of ῥυπάω, 'I am filthy'; the dirt is part of his beggar's guise. εἷμαι is the perfect middle of ἕννυμι 'clothe', 'I am clothed in, I wear', with the accusative εἵματα 'clothes'; κακὰ δὲ χροῒ εἵματα is 'bad clothes on my skin', χροΐ being the dative of χρώς 'skin, body'. τοὔνεκ’ is τοῦ ἕνεκα (τοῦ = τούτου) 'for that reason'. ἀτιμάζει is 'dishonours, slights'. οὔ πω is 'not yet'. In φησὶ τὸν εἶναι the article τόν is the pronoun 'him': she does not yet say that I am that man.

sentences.t: ἡμεῖς δὲ φραζώμεθ’ ὅπως ὄχ’ ἄριστα γένηται.
sentences.tr: hēmeis de phrazōmeth’ hopōs och’ arista genētai.
sentences.l: But let us consider how by far best it may come to be.
sentences.i: But let us consider how it may turn out best of all.
sentences.n: ἡμεῖς δέ sets the two men against Penelope. φραζώμεθ’ is the present subjunctive of φράζομαι 'consider, plan', a hortatory subjunctive, 'let us consider'. ὅπως with the subjunctive γένηται gives the content of the planning, 'how it may turn out'. ὄχ’ ἄριστα is 'by far the best': ὄχα is an intensifier used with superlatives (here with its final vowel elided), and ἄριστα is the neuter plural superlative of ἀγαθός.

sentences.t:
καὶ γάρ τίς θ’ ἕνα φῶτα κατακτείνας ἐνὶ δήμῳ,
ᾧ μὴ πολλοὶ ἔωσιν ἀοσσητῆρες ὀπίσσω,
φεύγει πηούς τε προλιπὼν καὶ πατρίδα γαῖαν·
sentences.tr:
kai gar tis th’ hena phōta katakteinas eni dēmōi,
hōi mē polloi eōsin aossētēres opissō,
pheugei pēous te prolipōn kai patrida gaian·
sentences.i: For even a man who has killed a single man in the land, and has not many helpers to come to his aid afterwards, goes into exile, leaving behind his relatives by marriage and his fatherland;
sentences.n: Odysseus first states an ordinary case, then applies it to themselves. καὶ γάρ is 'for even'. τίς θ’ is τίς τε: the epic τε marks a general statement, 'any man, as a rule'. ἕνα φῶτα is 'one man' (φώς 'man'), and κατακτείνας is the aorist participle of κατακτείνω 'kill'. ἐνὶ δήμῳ is 'in the land': δῆμος is the community of a district. ᾧ μὴ πολλοὶ ἔωσιν is a relative clause with μή and the subjunctive ἔωσιν (the epic subjunctive of εἰμί, = ὦσιν) because it is general: 'for whom there are not many'. ἀοσσητῆρες are 'helpers', and ὀπίσσω is 'hereafter, behind'. φεύγει is 'flees, goes into exile'. πηούς are relatives by marriage, and the unit ends at the · after πατρίδα γαῖαν, 'fatherland'.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δ’ ἕρμα πόληος ἀπέκταμεν, οἳ μέγ’ ἄριστοι
κούρων εἰν Ἰθάκῃ·
sentences.tr:
hēmeis d’ herma polēos apektamen, hoi meg’ aristoi
kourōn ein Ithakēi·
sentences.l:
but we have killed the prop of the city, who were by far the best
of the young men in Ithaca;
sentences.i: but we have killed the prop of the city, men who were by far the best of the young men in Ithaca;
sentences.n: ἕρμα is 'that which holds something up, a prop' (the word is also used of ballast and of a ship's support): a figure for the men who defended the city. ἀπέκταμεν is the aorist of ἀποκτείνω in its strong epic form (Attic ἀπεκτείναμεν); πόληος is the Ionic genitive of πόλις. The relative οἳ is plural although ἕρμα is singular, because it refers to the dead suitors: 'men who were by far the best'. μέγ’ ἄριστοι is 'by far the best' (μέγα as an intensifier with a superlative). κούρων is the genitive plural of κοῦρος 'young man', a partitive genitive, and εἰν is ἐν. The · after Ἰθάκῃ ends the unit in the middle of line 122.

sentences.t: τὰ δέ σε φράζεσθαι ἄνωγα.
sentences.tr: ta de se phrazesthai anōga.
sentences.l: and these things I bid you consider.”
sentences.i: These are the things I bid you consider.”
sentences.n: τὰ δέ is 'and these things': τά is the article used as a demonstrative pronoun. φράζεσθαι is the present infinitive middle of φράζομαι, depending on ἄνωγα. ἄνωγα 'I bid' is an old perfect with present sense, taking the accusative σε and an infinitive. Odysseus hands the problem of the killing to his son's thought, and the closing quotation mark falls here at the end of his speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: The reply formula for Telemachus. τὸν is 'him' and αὖ is 'in turn'; πεπνυμένος, 'prudent', is his stock epithet and is translated the same way every time; ἀντίον is the adverb 'face to face', and ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω 'speak'. It is not the same verb as the προσέφη of the line at 129.

sentences.t: αὐτὸς ταῦτά γε λεῦσσε, πάτερ φίλε·
sentences.tr: autos tauta ge leusse, pater phile·
sentences.l: “You yourself look to these things, dear father;
sentences.i: “Look to this yourself, dear father;
sentences.n: Telemachus answers his father. αὐτός is 'yourself'; ταῦτά γε is 'these things, at least'. λεῦσσε is the present imperative of λεύσσω 'look, see', used here for 'consider, look to'. πάτερ φίλε is 'dear father'. The · after φίλε ends the unit in the middle of line 124.

sentences.t:
σὴν γὰρ ἀρίστην
μῆτιν ἐπ’ ἀνθρώπους φάσ’ ἔμμεναι, οὐδέ κέ τίς τοι
ἄλλος ἀνὴρ ἐρίσειε καταθνητῶν ἀνθρώπων.
sentences.tr:
sēn gar aristēn
mētin ep’ anthrōpous phas’ emmenai, oude ke tis toi
allos anēr eriseie katathnētōn anthrōpōn.
sentences.l:
for your, the best
cunning among men they say it is, and not would any, to you,
other man rival, of mortal men.
sentences.i: for they say that your cunning is the best among men, and no other man among mortal men would rival you.
sentences.n: σήν is the possessive 'your'. μῆτις is 'cunning, craft'; it is the quality named in πολύμητις, the epithet of Odysseus in the formula at 129. φάσ’ is φασί 'they say', and ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί. ἐπ’ ἀνθρώπους is 'among men' (ἐπί with the accusative, of the group over which he stands). οὐδέ κέ τίς τοι ἄλλος ἀνὴρ ἐρίσειε is a potential optative, 'no other man would rival you': τοι is the epic enclitic dative of σύ (= σοί), ἐρίσειε the aorist optative of ἐρίζω 'compete with', and καταθνητῶν ἀνθρώπων 'of mortal men' is a genitive of the group.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δ’ ἐμμεμαῶτες ἅμ’ ἑψόμεθ’, οὐδέ τί φημι
ἀλκῆς δευήσεσθαι, ὅση δύναμίς γε πάρεστιν.
sentences.tr:
hēmeis d’ emmemaōtes ham’ hepsometh’, oude ti phēmi
alkēs deuēsesthai, hosē dynamis ge parestin.
sentences.l:
And we, eager, along with you will follow, and not at all, I say,
of might shall we fall short, as much as ability at least is at hand.”
sentences.i: And we shall follow with you eagerly, and I say that we shall not fall short in any way of might, so far as our ability goes.”
sentences.n: ἐμμεμαῶτες is a perfect participle, 'straining, eager', in the nominative plural with ἡμεῖς. ἅμ’ ἑψόμεθ’ is ἅμα ἑψόμεθα: ἅμα is 'along with', and ἑψόμεθα is the future of ἕπομαι 'follow'. οὐδέ τί φημι … δευήσεσθαι: φημί takes the future infinitive δευήσεσθαι (from δεύομαι 'lack, fall short of'), which takes the genitive ἀλκῆς 'of might'; in English the negative goes with the infinitive, 'I say we shall not fall short'. ὅση δύναμίς γε πάρεστιν is 'as much ability as is at hand'. The closing quotation mark falls here, at the end of Telemachus's speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: The reply formula for Odysseus. τὸν is 'him', ἀπαμειβόμενος is 'answering', and προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι 'speak to, address'. πολύμητις 'many-wiled' is his stock epithet, from πολυ- 'much' and μῆτις 'cunning'; it is translated the same way every time. Telemachus has just praised exactly that quality, and the next unit begins Odysseus's plan.

sentences.t: τοιγὰρ ἐγὼν ἐρέω ὥς μοι δοκεῖ εἶναι ἄριστα.
sentences.tr: toigar egōn ereō hōs moi dokei einai arista.
sentences.l: “Therefore I shall say as it seems to me to be best.
sentences.i: “Then I will tell you what seems to me best.
sentences.n: Odysseus's speech begins. τοιγάρ is 'therefore, well then'. ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ. ἐρέω is the uncontracted future of the verb 'say' (Attic ἐρῶ). ὡς … δοκεῖ is 'as it seems': δοκεῖ is the third person singular of δοκέω, with the dative μοι 'to me', and εἶναι ἄριστα is 'to be best' (neuter plural superlative of ἀγαθός). The plan follows in order.

sentences.t:
πρῶτα μὲν ἂρ λούσασθε καὶ ἀμφιέσασθε χιτῶνας,
δμῳὰς δ’ ἐν μεγάροισιν ἀνώγετε εἵμαθ’ ἑλέσθαι·
sentences.tr:
prōta men ar lousasthe kai amphiesasthe chitōnas,
dmōias d’ en megaroisin anōgete heimath’ helesthai·
sentences.l:
First, then, wash and put on tunics,
and the maidservants in the halls bid to take clothes;
sentences.i: First, then, bathe and put on your tunics, and bid the maids in the halls to take up their clothes;
sentences.n: πρῶτα μέν begins a list of steps; the matching αὐτάρ comes in the next unit. λούσασθε and ἀμφιέσασθε are aorist imperatives middle (second person plural) of λούω 'wash' and ἀμφιέννυμι 'put on', with the accusative χιτῶνας 'tunics'. δμῳάς is the accusative plural of δμῳή 'maidservant'. ἀνώγετε is the present imperative plural of ἀνώγω 'bid', the same verb as ἄνωγα at 122, and governs δμῳάς with the aorist infinitive ἑλέσθαι 'to take'. εἵματα are 'clothes'. The order is: the men wash and dress, and the women dress too.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ θεῖος ἀοιδὸς ἔχων φόρμιγγα λίγειαν
ἡμῖν ἡγείσθω φιλοπαίγμονος ὀρχηθμοῖο,
ὥς κέν τις φαίη γάμον ἔμμεναι ἐκτὸς ἀκούων,
ἢ ἀν’ ὁδὸν στείχων, ἢ οἳ περιναιετάουσι·
sentences.tr:
autar theios aoidos echōn phorminga ligeian
hēmin hēgeisthō philopaigmonos orchēthmoio,
hōs ken tis phaiē gamon emmenai ektos akouōn,
ē an’ hodon steichōn, ē hoi perinaietaousi·
sentences.i: And then let the divine minstrel, holding the clear-sounding lyre, lead for us a dance that delights in play, so that someone hearing it from outside, whether going along the road or one of those who live round about, may say that there is a wedding;
sentences.n: The second step of the plan: the noise of a dance is to hide what has happened. αὐτάρ is 'and then', answering πρῶτα μέν in 131. θεῖος ἀοιδός is the stock phrase 'divine minstrel', and φόρμιγξ λίγεια is 'the clear-sounding lyre'. ἡγείσθω is the present imperative third person singular of ἡγέομαι 'lead', with the dative ἡμῖν 'for us' and the genitive ὀρχηθμοῖο 'the dance'. φιλοπαίγμων is built from φίλος 'loving' and παίζω 'play'. The purpose clause ὥς κέν τις φαίη is ὡς + κεν + the optative of φημί, 'so that someone might say'; γάμον ἔμμεναι is 'that there is a wedding'. ἐκτὸς ἀκούων is 'hearing from outside'. The next line names two kinds of hearer: ἀν’ ὁδὸν στείχων (ἀνά with the accusative, 'going along the road') and οἳ περιναιετάουσι 'those who live round about', with the uncontracted ending -άουσι.

sentences.t:
μὴ πρόσθε κλέος εὐρὺ φόνου κατὰ ἄστυ γένηται
ἀνδρῶν μνηστήρων, πρίν γ’ ἡμέας ἐλθέμεν ἔξω
ἀγρὸν ἐς ἡμέτερον πολυδένδρεον·
sentences.tr:
mē prosthe kleos eury phonou kata asty genētai
andrōn mnēstērōn, prin g’ hēmeas elthemen exō
agron es hēmeteron polydendreon·
sentences.i: so that no wide report of the slaughter of the suitors spreads through the town before we have gone out to our own farm, rich in trees;
sentences.n: μή with the subjunctive γένηται gives a negative purpose, 'lest it arise'. κλέος εὐρύ is 'wide fame': κλέος is 'what is heard of someone', and here it is only the news. φόνου is 'of the slaughter'. πρίν γ’ ἡμέας ἐλθέμεν ἔξω is πρίν with an infinitive and an accusative subject, 'before we go out': ἡμέας is the Ionic accusative of ἡμεῖς, and ἐλθέμεν is the epic infinitive in -έμεν. ἀγρὸν ἐς ἡμέτερον πολυδένδρεον is 'to our own farm, rich in trees', from πολυ- 'much' and δένδρον 'tree'. The · after πολυδένδρεον ends the unit in the middle of line 139.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἔπειτα
φρασσόμεθ’ ὅττι κε κέρδος Ὀλύμπιος ἐγγυαλίξῃ.
sentences.tr:
entha d’ epeita
phrassometh’ hotti ke kerdos Olympios engyalixēi.
sentences.l:
and there then
we shall consider what gain the Olympian may put into our hands.”
sentences.i: and there, after that, we shall consider what advantage the Olympian may put into our hands.”
sentences.n: ἔνθα δ’ ἔπειτα is 'and there, after that'. φρασσόμεθα is the future of φράζομαι 'consider'. ὅττι κε … ἐγγυαλίξῃ is an indefinite relative clause with κε and the aorist subjunctive of ἐγγυαλίζω 'put into the hands of'; κέρδος is 'gain, advantage'. Ὀλύμπιος alone, 'the Olympian', is the god who lives on Olympus, here Zeus, who is not named. The closing quotation mark falls here, at the end of Odysseus's speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα τοῦ μάλα μὲν κλύον ἠδ’ ἐπίθοντο,
πρῶτα μὲν οὖν λούσαντο καὶ ἀμφιέσαντο χιτῶνας,
ὅπλισθεν δὲ γυναῖκες·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara tou mala men klyon ēd’ epithonto,
prōta men oun lousanto kai amphiesanto chitōnas,
hoplisthen de gynaikes·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they listened to him readily and obeyed. First they washed and put on tunics, and the women got ready;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ὣς ἔφατο 'so he spoke', with ἔφατο elided before the rough breathing of οἱ. οἱ δέ … ἐπίθοντο is 'and they obeyed': κλύον 'heard' takes the pronoun τοῦ, 'him', in the genitive, as verbs of hearing do; ἐπίθοντο, the aorist middle of πείθομαι 'obey', has the same 'him' understood. The three clauses make one unit: they obey, the men wash and dress, and the women do the same. ὅπλισθεν is the aorist passive of ὁπλίζω 'make ready' with the ending -θεν for -θησαν; here it means that the women dressed themselves. The · after γυναῖκες ends the unit in the middle of line 143.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ εἵλετο θεῖος ἀοιδὸς
φόρμιγγα γλαφυρήν, ἐν δέ σφισιν ἵμερον ὦρσε
μολπῆς τε γλυκερῆς καὶ ἀμύμονος ὀρχηθμοῖο.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ heileto theios aoidos
phorminga glaphyrēn, en de sphisin himeron ōrse
molpēs te glykerēs kai amymonos orchēthmoio.
sentences.l:
and he took, the divine minstrel,
the hollow lyre, and in them he aroused a longing
for sweet song-and-dance and for blameless dancing.
sentences.i: and the divine minstrel took up the hollow lyre and stirred in them a longing for sweet song and dance and for blameless dancing.
sentences.n: In ὁ δ’ εἵλετο θεῖος ἀοιδός, ὁ is the pronoun 'he' and θεῖος ἀοιδός is in apposition. εἵλετο is the aorist middle of αἱρέω 'take'. φόρμιγξ γλαφυρή is 'the hollow lyre'. ἐν δέ σφισιν ἵμερον ὦρσε is 'and he aroused in them a longing': ἐν is adverbial, σφισιν is the dative plural 'them', and ὦρσε is the aorist of ὄρνυμι 'rouse'. ἵμερος takes the genitives μολπῆς and ὀρχηθμοῖο, 'for song-and-dance, for dancing'; μολπή is song that goes with dance. ἀμύμων, 'blameless', is a stock epithet whose real meaning is not known: 'faultless' is the traditional guess, and the ancient commentators disagreed.

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δὲ μέγα δῶμα περιστεναχίζετο ποσσὶν
ἀνδρῶν παιζόντων καλλιζώνων τε γυναικῶν.
sentences.tr:
toisin de mega dōma peristenachizeto possin
andrōn paizontōn kallizōnōn te gynaikōn.
sentences.l:
And around them the great house resounded with the feet
of men playing and of fair-girdled women.
sentences.i: And all about them the great house resounded with the feet of men at play and of fair-girdled women.
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is a dative of interest, 'for them'; the sense 'around them' comes from the περι- in the verb. περιστεναχίζετο is the imperfect middle of περιστεναχίζω, 'resound all round' (στεναχίζω is 'groan, sigh', and here the house itself groans under the beat of the feet). ποσσίν is the dative plural of πούς 'foot', with the ending -σσι. παιζόντων is the genitive plural of the participle of παίζω 'play, make merry', and agrees with ἀνδρῶν. καλλιζώνων is 'fair-girdled', from καλλι- 'fair' and ζώνη 'girdle'; the epithet is translated the same way every time.

sentences.t: ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκε δόμων ἔκτοσθεν ἀκούων·
sentences.tr: hōde de tis eipeske domōn ektosthen akouōn·
sentences.l: And thus someone would say, hearing from outside the house:
sentences.i: And someone outside the house, hearing it, would say:
sentences.n: The line introduces the remark of a bystander, which shows that the pretence works. ὧδε is 'in this way' and points forward. εἴπεσκε has the iterative suffix -σκε, 'would say', each passer-by or neighbour in turn. δόμων ἔκτοσθεν is 'from outside the house': ἔκτοσθεν takes the genitive. ἀκούων is 'hearing'. The · introduces the quoted words.

sentences.t: ἦ μάλα δή τις ἔγημε πολυμνήστην βασίλειαν·
sentences.tr: ē mala dē tis egēme polymnēstēn basileian·
sentences.l: “Truly indeed someone has married the much-wooed queen;
sentences.i: “Surely someone has married the much-wooed queen;
sentences.n: The speaker is not named. ἦ μάλα δή is a strong exclamation, 'truly indeed'. ἔγημε is the aorist of γαμέω, said of a man, 'married'. πολυμνήστην is 'much-wooed' (πολυ- 'much' and a verbal adjective of μνάομαι 'woo'), and βασίλειαν is 'queen'. The passer-by assumes that Penelope has taken one of the suitors as her husband.

sentences.t:
σχετλίη, οὐδ’ ἔτλη πόσιος οὗ κουριδίοιο
εἴρυσθαι μέγα δῶμα διαμπερές, ἧος ἵκοιτο.
sentences.tr:
schetliē, oud’ etlē posios hou kouridioio
eirysthai mega dōma diamperes, hēos hikoito.
sentences.l:
Cruel one! and she did not bring herself, of her own wedded husband,
to guard the great house continually, until he should come.”
sentences.i: Cruel woman! She did not bring herself to guard the great house of her own wedded husband continually, until he came back.”
sentences.n: σχετλίη is the feminine of σχέτλιος, 'cruel one', an exclamation of reproach. οὐδ’ ἔτλη is 'and she did not bring herself': ἔτλη is the aorist of τλῆναι, and it takes the infinitive εἴρυσθαι (= ἐρύσθαι), 'to guard'. πόσιος οὗ κουριδίοιο: οὗ is the possessive 'her own', not the relative, and κουριδίοιο, a genitive in -οιο, is 'wedded'; the genitive depends on δῶμα, 'the great house of her own wedded husband', and stands ahead of the infinitive. διαμπερές is 'continually, right through'. ἧος … ἵκοιτο is 'until he should come': ἧος is the epic form of ἕως, and ἵκοιτο the optative of ἵκω. The closing quotation mark falls here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα τις εἴπεσκε, τὰ δ’ οὐκ ἴσαν ὡς ἐτέτυκτο.
sentences.tr: hōs ara tis eipeske, ta d’ ouk isan hōs etetykto.
sentences.l: So then someone would say, but they did not know how it had been contrived.
sentences.i: So one of them would say, not knowing how matters really stood.
sentences.n: The narrator closes the bystander's remark with the formula that says he is wrong. ὣς ἄρα is 'so then'; τις εἴπεσκε is 'someone would say', with the iterative suffix -σκε. τὰ δ’ οὐκ ἴσαν ὡς ἐτέτυκτο is 'but they did not know how things had been contrived': τά is the pronoun 'those things', ἴσαν is the epic third person plural of οἶδα (used as an imperfect; Attic ᾔδεσαν), and ἐτέτυκτο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω 'make, contrive'. The people outside did not know how matters had been arranged.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσῆα μεγαλήτορα ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ
Εὐρυνόμη ταμίη λοῦσεν καὶ χρῖσεν ἐλαίῳ,
ἀμφὶ δέ μιν φᾶρος καλὸν βάλεν ἠδὲ χιτῶνα·
sentences.tr:
autar Odyssēa megalētora hōi eni oikōi
Eurynomē tamiē lousen kai chrisen elaiōi,
amphi de min pharos kalon balen ēde chitōna·
sentences.i: But in his own house Eurynome the housekeeper washed great-spirited Odysseus and anointed him with oil, and threw a fine cloak and a tunic about him;
sentences.n: The narrative goes back inside. αὐτάρ is 'but, and'. Ὀδυσσῆα μεγαλήτορα is 'great-spirited Odysseus': μεγαλήτωρ is a stock epithet, translated every time, and Ὀδυσσῆα, the accusative, is the object of the verbs. ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ is 'in his own house': ᾧ is the possessive 'his own', not the relative. Εὐρυνόμη ταμίη is 'Eurynome the housekeeper'. λοῦσεν and χρῖσεν are the aorists of λούω 'wash' and χρίω 'anoint'; ἐλαίῳ is 'with oil'. φᾶρος is a cloak, here a man's, and χιτών a tunic; ἀμφὶ δέ μιν … βάλεν is 'and threw about him', with the preposition separated from its verb (tmesis).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ κὰκ κεφαλῆς κάλλος πολὺ χεῦεν Ἀθήνη
μείζονά τ’ εἰσιδέειν καὶ πάσσονα·
sentences.tr:
autar kak kephalēs kallos poly cheuen Athēnē
meizona t’ eisideein kai passona·
sentences.l:
And down from his head beauty abundant poured Athena,
taller to look upon and thicker;
sentences.i: And Athena poured abundant beauty down from his head, making him taller to look at and sturdier;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is 'and then'. κὰκ κεφαλῆς is κατὰ κεφαλῆς, with the final α of the preposition dropped and the τ assimilated to the κ that follows: 'down from the head'. κάλλος πολύ is 'much beauty'. χεῦεν is the aorist of χέω 'pour'. Ἀθήνη is the Ionic form of the name. The accusatives μείζονα 'taller' and πάσσονα 'thicker, stouter' (the comparative of παχύς) have no noun beside them: they go with Odysseus, the understood object. εἰσιδέειν is the uncontracted aorist infinitive of εἰσοράω, 'to look at'. The · after πάσσονα ends the unit in the middle of line 157.

sentences.t:
κὰδ δὲ κάρητος
οὔλας ἧκε κόμας, ὑακινθίνῳ ἄνθει ὁμοίας.
sentences.tr:
kad de karētos
oulas hēke komas, hyakinthinōi anthei homoias.
sentences.l:
and down from his head
she sent curling locks, like the hyacinth flower.
sentences.i: and she let curling locks fall from his head, like the hyacinth flower.
sentences.n: κὰδ δὲ κάρητος is κατὰ δὲ κάρητος, 'and down from the head': κάρητος is the genitive of κάρη 'head'. οὔλας … κόμας is 'curling locks' (οὖλος is 'woolly, curled'). ἧκε is the aorist of ἵημι 'send, let fall'. ὑακινθίνῳ ἄνθει ὁμοίας is 'like the hyacinth flower': ὁμοίας agrees with κόμας and takes the dative, and ὑακίνθινος means 'of the hyacinth'. Which flower the Greek ὑάκινθος was is not certain.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε τις χρυσὸν περιχεύεται ἀργύρῳ ἀνὴρ
ἴδρις, ὃν Ἥφαιστος δέδαεν καὶ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη
τέχνην παντοίην, χαρίεντα δὲ ἔργα τελείει·
ὣς μὲν τῷ περίχευε χάριν κεφαλῇ τε καὶ ὤμοις.
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hote tis chryson pericheuetai argyrōi anēr
idris, hon Hēphaistos dedaen kai Pallas Athēnē
technēn pantoiēn, charienta de erga teleiei·
hōs men tōi pericheue charin kephalēi te kai ōmois.
sentences.l:
And as when a man pours gold about silver,
skilled, one whom Hephaestus taught and Pallas Athena
every craft, and graceful works he brings to completion,
so indeed on him she poured-around a grace, on head and on shoulders.
sentences.i: As when a skilled man overlays silver with gold, one whom Hephaestus and Pallas Athena have taught every craft, and he brings graceful works to completion, so she shed a grace about his head and shoulders.
sentences.n: A simile: Athena's gift to Odysseus is compared to a craftsman's gilding. ὡς δ’ ὅτε is 'and as when'. περιχεύεται is the present middle of περιχέω, 'pours around', with the accusative χρυσόν 'gold' and the dative ἀργύρῳ 'silver': a craftsman pours gold about silver. ἴδρις is 'skilled, knowing'. In ὃν Ἥφαιστος δέδαεν the ὅν is the relative 'whom', not the possessive: δέδαεν is the reduplicated aorist of διδάσκω 'teach', and τέχνην παντοίην 'every kind of craft' is its second accusative. Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη is 'Pallas Athena'; the meaning of Παλλάς is disputed. τελείει is the present of τελέω with the lengthened Homeric spelling. The comparison closes with ὣς: περίχευε is the aorist of the same verb περιχέω, so the grace is a gilding poured about him; τῷ is the article as pronoun, 'on him'. κεφαλῇ τε καὶ ὤμοις is 'on head and on shoulders'.

sentences.t: ἐκ δ’ ἀσαμίνθου βῆ δέμας ἀθανάτοισιν ὁμοῖος·
sentences.tr: ek d’ asaminthou bē demas athanatoisin homoios·
sentences.l: and out of the bath he stepped, in body like the immortals;
sentences.i: and he stepped out of the bath, in body like the immortals;
sentences.n: ἐκ δ’ … βῆ is a tmesis: ἐκ and βῆ are one verb, 'stepped out'. βῆ is the aorist of βαίνω without the augment. ἀσάμινθος is 'bath, bath-tub'. δέμας is an accusative of respect, 'in body, in form'. ἀθανάτοισιν ὁμοῖος is 'like the immortals', ὁμοῖος taking the dative. After the gifts of Athena, the beggar has gone from sight.

sentences.t:
ἂψ δ’ αὖτις κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετ’ ἐπὶ θρόνου ἔνθεν ἀνέστη,
ἀντίον ἧς ἀλόχου, καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπε·
sentences.tr:
aps d’ autis kat’ ar’ hezet’ epi thronou enthen anestē,
antion hēs alochou, kai min pros mython eeipe·
sentences.l:
And back again he sat down upon the chair from which he had risen,
opposite his own wife, and her with a word he addressed:
sentences.i: He went back and sat down again on the chair he had risen from, opposite his own wife, and spoke to her:
sentences.n: ἂψ δ’ αὖτις is 'and back again'. κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετ’ is a tmesis for κατέζετο 'sat down' (ἕζετο is a past tense of ἕζομαι); ἐπὶ θρόνου ἔνθεν ἀνέστη is 'on the chair from which he had risen', ἔνθεν meaning 'from where' and ἀνέστη being the aorist of ἀνίστημι in its intransitive sense; θρόνος is 'chair'. ἀντίον ἧς ἀλόχου is 'opposite his own wife': ἧς is the possessive 'his own' (ὅς, not the relative) and ἀντίον takes the genitive. καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπε is 'and spoke to her': πρὸς … ἔειπε is a tmesis for προσεῖπε. The · ends the unit; Odysseus's speech follows.

sentences.t:
δαιμονίη, περί σοί γε γυναικῶν θηλυτεράων
κῆρ ἀτέραμνον ἔθηκαν Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχοντες·
sentences.tr:
daimoniē, peri soi ge gynaikōn thēlyteraōn
kēr ateramnon ethēkan Olympia dōmat’ echontes·
sentences.l:
“Strange woman, beyond, for you at least, of women, the female ones,
a heart unsoftened made those who hold the Olympian halls;
sentences.i: “Strange woman, those who hold the halls of Olympus have made your heart more unyielding than that of any other woman;
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks to Penelope. δαιμονίη is the feminine of δαιμόνιος, an address that mixes surprise with reproach; its exact force is uncertain ('strange one'). περί σοί γε γυναικῶν θηλυτεράων: περί is 'beyond' and takes the genitive γυναικῶν, 'than women'; σοί is 'in your case'; θηλυτεράων, an uncontracted genitive plural (Attic -ῶν), is 'female' and is a comparative in form only. κῆρ with a circumflex is 'heart', a different word from κήρ 'death-spirit'. ἀτέραμνον is 'unsoftened, hard': ἀ- 'not' and a word for 'soft' (compare τέρην) is the usual explanation, though the formation is not certain. ἔθηκαν is the aorist of τίθημι 'make, put'. Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχοντες is a periphrasis for the gods, 'those who hold the Olympian halls'; the plural δώματα stands for one dwelling.

sentences.t:
οὐ μέν κ’ ἄλλη γ’ ὧδε γυνὴ τετληότι θυμῷ
ἀνδρὸς ἀφεσταίη, ὅς οἱ κακὰ πολλὰ μογήσας
ἔλθοι ἐεικοστῷ ἔτεϊ ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.tr:
ou men k’ allē g’ hōde gynē tetlēoti thymōi
andros aphestaiē, hos hoi kaka polla mogēsas
elthoi eeikostōi eteï es patrida gaian.
sentences.i: No other woman would hold aloof from her husband like this, with an enduring heart, when he had come to his fatherland in the twentieth year after toiling through many evils;
sentences.n: These three lines are the same as lines 100 to 102, which Telemachus said to his mother; now Odysseus says them, ending with a full stop, and the English is kept the same word for word. Father and son make the same charge. οὐ μέν κε … ἀφεσταίη is a potential optative, 'would not … stand aloof', and ἀφεσταίη takes the genitive ἀνδρός. τετληότι θυμῷ is 'with enduring heart'. ὅς … ἔλθοι is a relative clause with the optative, and the dative οἱ is a dative of interest that English drops; whom it points to the Greek leaves open. μογήσας is 'having toiled through'. ἐεικοστῷ ἔτεϊ is 'in the twentieth year'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι, μαῖα, στόρεσον λέχος, ὄφρα καὶ αὐτὸς
λέξομαι·
sentences.tr:
all’ age moi, maia, storeson lechos, ophra kai autos
lexomai·
sentences.l:
But come, for me, nurse, spread a bed, so that I too, myself,
may lie down;
sentences.i: But come, nurse, spread a bed for me, so that I too may lie down;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is 'but come', and μοι is the dative 'for me'. μαῖα is the vocative of a respectful address to an older woman, 'nurse'; Penelope's answer at 177 sends Eurycleia to do the same task. στόρεσον is the aorist imperative of στορέννυμι 'spread', and λέχος is 'bed' in the sense of the bedstead. ὄφρα καὶ αὐτὸς λέξομαι is 'so that I too myself may lie down': λέξομαι belongs to λέγομαι 'lie down', and after ὄφρα it is a short-vowel subjunctive or a future. The · after λέξομαι ends the unit in the middle of line 172.

sentences.t: ἦ γὰρ τῇ γε σιδήρεον ἐν φρεσὶ ἦτορ.
sentences.tr: ē gar tēi ge sidēreon en phresi ētor.
sentences.l: for truly, to her, at least, of iron is the heart in her mind.”
sentences.i: for the heart in her mind is surely iron.”
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ gives his reason, 'for truly': he asks for a bed of his own because her heart is iron. τῇ is the article used as a pronoun, 'to her', a dative of possession, and γε is 'at least'. σιδήρεον is 'of iron' (σίδηρος 'iron'); it answers Telemachus's 'harder than stone' at 103. ἐν φρεσί is 'in the mind' (φρεσί is the dative plural of φρήν), and ἦτορ is 'heart'. The closing quotation mark falls here, at the end of Odysseus's speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe periphrōn Pēnelopeia·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The same formula as at 104, and the English is the same. Penelope now answers her husband. τὸν is 'him', αὖτε 'in turn', προσέειπε 'addressed', and περίφρων 'circumspect' is her stock epithet.

sentences.t:
δαιμόνι’, οὔτ’ ἄρ τι μεγαλίζομαι οὔτ’ ἀθερίζω
οὔτε λίην ἄγαμαι, μάλα δ’ εὖ οἶδ’ οἷος ἔησθα
ἐξ Ἰθάκης ἐπὶ νηὸς ἰὼν δολιχηρέτμοιο.
sentences.tr:
daimoni’, out’ ar ti megalizomai out’ atherizō
oute liēn agamai, mala d’ eu oid’ hoios eēstha
ex Ithakēs epi nēos iōn dolichēretmoio.
sentences.l:
“Strange man, neither at all do I exalt myself, nor do I make light of you,
nor do I marvel overmuch, but very well I know what sort of man you were
from Ithaca, on a ship going, a long-oared one.
sentences.i: “Strange man, I am not giving myself airs, nor am I thinking little of you, nor am I overly amazed, but I know very well what sort of man you were when you left Ithaca in a long-oared ship.
sentences.n: Penelope answers her husband. δαιμόνι’ is the masculine vocative of δαιμόνιος (elided), the counterpart of δαιμονίη at 166. οὔτ’ ἄρ τι is 'neither at all' (ἄρ is ἄρα). She names three attitudes and disowns each: μεγαλίζομαι 'I exalt myself, give myself airs' (the middle of μεγαλίζω), ἀθερίζω 'I make light of' (with 'you' understood), and ἄγαμαι 'I marvel at'; λίην is 'too much'. μάλα δ’ εὖ οἶδα is 'but I know very well'. οἷος ἔησθα is 'what sort of man you were': ἔησθα is the uncontracted second person singular imperfect of εἰμί (Attic ἦσθα). ἐξ Ἰθάκης ἐπὶ νηὸς ἰὼν δολιχηρέτμοιο is 'going from Ithaca on a long-oared ship': ἰών is the participle of εἶμι 'go', and δολιχηρέτμοιο (a genitive in -οιο) is 'long-oared'. She says she holds a memory of the man who left, and that this is what she measures him against.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε οἱ στόρεσον πυκινὸν λέχος, Εὐρύκλεια,
ἐκτὸς ἐϋσταθέος θαλάμου, τόν ῥ’ αὐτὸς ἐποίει·
sentences.tr:
all’ age hoi storeson pykinon lechos, Eurykleia,
ektos eÿstatheos thalamou, ton rh’ autos epoiei·
sentences.l:
But come, for him spread the solid bed, Eurycleia,
outside the well-standing chamber, which he himself made;
sentences.i: But come, Eurycleia, spread the solid bed for him outside the sturdy chamber, the one he built himself;
sentences.n: Penelope turns to Eurycleia, named here by the vocative Εὐρύκλεια. οἱ is the dative 'for him', and στόρεσον is the same imperative as at 171. πυκινὸν λέχος is 'the solid bed': πυκινός is 'solid, close-built'. ἐκτὸς ἐϋσταθέος θαλάμου is 'outside the well-standing chamber': ἐκτός takes the genitive, ἐϋσταθής is 'well-standing, sturdy', and θάλαμος is the inner room. τόν ῥ’ αὐτὸς ἐποίει: τόν is masculine, so its antecedent is θαλάμου, not the neuter λέχος, and the clause says that he made the chamber himself; ῥ’ is the particle ῥα, and ἐποίει the imperfect of ποιέω 'make, build'. Line 181 tells us that she is testing him.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα οἱ ἐκθεῖσαι πυκινὸν λέχος ἐμβάλετ’ εὐνήν,
κώεα καὶ χλαίνας καὶ ῥήγεα σιγαλόεντα.
sentences.tr:
entha hoi ektheisai pykinon lechos embalet’ eunēn,
kōea kai chlainas kai rhēgea sigaloenta.
sentences.l:
There for him, having put out the solid bed, throw on a couch,
fleeces and cloaks and glossy rugs.”
sentences.i: Once you have put the solid bed out there for him, make up a couch on it, with fleeces and cloaks and glossy rugs.”
sentences.n: ἔνθα is 'there'. οἱ is 'for him'. ἐκθεῖσαι is the aorist participle, feminine plural, of ἐκτίθημι 'set out', and ἐμβάλετ’ is the second person plural imperative of ἐμβάλλω 'throw in, put on'; both are plural, so the order passes from Eurycleia to the women who work with her. λέχος and εὐνή are two words: the λέχος is the bedstead and the εὐνή what is laid on it. κώεα καὶ χλαίνας καὶ ῥήγεα σιγαλόεντα, 'fleeces and cloaks and glossy rugs', stand in apposition to εὐνήν and list the bedding; κώεα is the plural of κῶας 'fleece', and σιγαλόεις is 'glossy'. The closing quotation mark falls here, at the end of Penelope's speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη πόσιος πειρωμένη·
sentences.tr: hōs ar’ ephē posios peirōmenē·
sentences.l: So then she spoke, her husband testing;
sentences.i: So she spoke, testing her husband;
sentences.n: The narrator tells us how to read what she has just said. ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη is 'so then she spoke', ἔφη being the third person singular of φημί. πειρωμένη is the present middle participle of πειράω 'try, test', and takes the genitive πόσιος 'husband' (πόσις, with the epic genitive πόσιος). It is the same verb (πειράω beside πειράζω) as πειράζειν ἐμέθεν at 114, where Odysseus told Telemachus to let his mother 'make trial of him': the test he expected has now been set. The · after πειρωμένη ends the unit in the middle of line 181.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ὀχθήσας ἄλοχον προσεφώνεε κεδνὰ ἰδυῖαν·
sentences.tr:
autar Odysseus
ochthēsas alochon prosephōnee kedna iduian·
sentences.l:
but Odysseus,
vexed, spoke to his wife, the one wise and trusty:
sentences.i: but Odysseus, troubled, spoke to his wife, trusty and wise:
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is 'but'. ὀχθήσας is the aorist participle of ὀχθέω 'be vexed, troubled'. προσεφώνεε is the imperfect of προσφωνέω 'speak to', and ἄλοχον is its object. κεδνὰ ἰδυῖαν is a stock epithet of the wife, translated every time: ἰδυῖαν is the feminine accusative of the perfect participle of οἶδα, 'knowing', and κεδνά is 'trusty things', so 'the one wise and trusty'. The line ends in ·, and the speech it introduces begins in the next part, so no quotation mark stands here.
